name: Danaher Leg Lock System

products.title: Leglocks: Enter The System
products.blurb: Connects inside position, ashi garami entries, knee-line control and leg attacks in a structured curriculum.
products.best_for: No-gi students who want to understand control before adding more leg-lock entries.
products.study_focus: Start with the inside-position and knee-line sections before studying the entry variations.
products.practice_tip: With your coach, choose one entry and practise retaining the position while your partner works to free the knee. Reset before applying submission pressure.

description: Connects inside position, ashi garami entries, knee-line control and leg attacks in a structured curriculum. Explore the training sequence and course on BJJ Fanatics.
summary: A leg entry is useful only if you can retain control when your partner moves.
overview:
A leg entry is useful only if you can retain control when your partner moves. This guide organizes ashi garami around inside position, knee-line retention and transitions between entanglements. The aim is to recognize when to hold, adjust or disengage before attempting a submission.

Use the implementation sequence to choose a training focus, the connected techniques to study each position, and the course recommendation to explore a detailed video explanation. This is BJJGraph’s study guide; it is not an official course outline or a substitute for coached practice.
key_principles: Control Before Submission - Retain the entanglement before adding finishing pressure
Recognize the Position - Distinguish standard ashi, outside ashi and 50/50
Knee-Line Retention - Understand when the opponent can withdraw the knee
Manage Rotation - Recognize how movement changes the available controls
Build One Entry - Connect a familiar guard to a position you can maintain
Train Defense Alongside Attack - Recognize early escape opportunities with your coach
Use Controlled Practice - Reset when control is lost and release immediately on a tap

key_components.description: Ashi garami describes a family of leg entanglements. Standard ashi, outside ashi and 50/50 have different control problems; 50/50 is not another name for outside ashi. Inside sankaku is also commonly called the saddle or honey hole, rather than being a separate step above them. Choose transitions based on knee-line control, rotation and the opponent’s available defenses.
key_components.purpose: Establish clear positional objectives and advancement pathways in leg entanglements

key_components.description: Systematic entries to leg entanglements are established through guard passing sequences, X-guard transitions, and seated guard engagements. The system teaches specific pathways from common positions like single leg X-guard, de la riva guard, and headquarters position into various ashi-garami configurations. This integration ensures practitioners can reliably access leg entanglements rather than waiting for opportunistic moments.
key_components.purpose: Create reliable pathways from common positions to leg entanglement control

key_components.description: Finishing details depend on the submission and entanglement. Study them with a qualified coach after positional control is established. Retain the opponent’s knee line during the setup, avoid uncontrolled rotation, and release immediately on a tap.
key_components.purpose: Connect positional control to supervised submission practice

key_components.description: The system includes comprehensive transition sequences between different ashi-garami positions, allowing practitioners to advance the hierarchy when opponents defend or to switch attack angles when direct finishing is blocked. Key transitions include outside ashi to standard ashi, standard ashi to inside ashi, cross ashi entries, and the critical advancement to saddle position. Understanding these pathways prevents stagnation and enables systematic position improvement.
key_components.purpose: Enable dynamic position advancement and attack angle variation within leg entanglements

common_obstacles.obstacle: Chasing a finish before controlling the position
common_obstacles.solution: Start rounds with positional retention as the goal. Ask your partner to withdraw the knee, and reset when they escape rather than holding a finishing grip through uncontrolled movement.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Entry Difficulty - Practitioners struggle to reliably enter ashi-garami positions against aware opponents
common_obstacles.solution: Develop systematic entry sequences from common positions rather than isolated techniques. Focus on single leg X-guard as primary gateway position, practice seated guard pulls with immediate leg entanglement, and integrate ashi entries into existing guard passing sequences to create multiple pathways.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Treating every entanglement as a fixed step on a ladder
common_obstacles.solution: Study the control problem in the position you have. Outside ashi and 50/50 can have useful attacks; a transition is a choice based on the opponent’s defense, not a requirement to reach a single ideal position.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Defense Ignorance - Lack of understanding defensive priorities leads to dangerous training situations and injury risk
common_obstacles.solution: Mandate comprehensive defensive instruction parallel to offensive system development. Ensure all practitioners understand inside heel exposure defense, safe rolling directions, and tap-early protocols. Establish training culture that prioritizes long-term safety over short-term submission success.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Confusing attacking control with defensive escape
common_obstacles.solution: The attacker generally wants to retain the opponent’s knee line, while the defender seeks to free it. Ask your coach to distinguish those roles before practising the details of an individual submission.

training_methodology.drilling_approach: The Danaher Leg Lock System requires progressive, systematic drilling that builds from isolated mechanics to integrated sequences. Begin with positional drilling focusing on establishing and maintaining control in each ashi-garami position without submission attempts. Progress to transition drilling between positions, emphasizing smooth advancement through the hierarchy. Only after control and transition mechanics are solid should breaking sequences be introduced, initially with compliant partners and gradually increasing resistance. Finishing mechanics are practiced last, always emphasizing control maintenance over explosive submission attempts. Defensive drilling must be trained in parallel, ensuring all participants understand inside heel exposure defense and safe escape protocols before attempting advanced positions.

progression_path.focus: Conceptual understanding, basic entries, standard ashi-garami control establishment
Movement between ashi-garami positions, hierarchy advancement, defensive fundamentals
Systematic leg straightening, bite point achievement, submission setup without finishing

Strategic implementation, entry timing, position recognition under resistance

common_mistakes: Chasing a submission after losing the knee line
Treating 50/50 and outside ashi as the same position
Treating the saddle and inside sankaku as separate steps in a fixed hierarchy
Adding resistance before understanding the position
Using speed or force to compensate for lost control

flashcards.question: What is the core organizing principle of the Danaher Leg Lock System?
flashcards.answer: It treats ashi-garami leg entanglements as positions in a control hierarchy. You must establish dominant control and advance position before attempting any submission, applying the same position-before-submission logic used for mount or back control.

flashcards.question: How are outside ashi, 50/50 and inside sankaku related?
flashcards.answer: Outside ashi and 50/50 are distinct entanglements. Inside sankaku is also commonly called the saddle or honey hole. Their usefulness depends on control and the opponent’s defenses rather than a fixed ladder.
flashcards.answer_line: Distinct positions; saddle is inside sankaku

plausible: 50/50 is another name for outside ashi
The saddle is a step below inside sankaku

flashcards.question: What should be checked before adding a leg-lock finishing setup?
flashcards.answer: Check knee-line retention, control of movement and the requirements of the specific submission with your coach. If the partner can withdraw the knee or rotate beyond your control, reset or recover position.
flashcards.answer_line: Retain knee line and control movement

plausible: Hold the heel while they freely rotate
trap: Finish faster when control is lost

flashcards.question: Why is the single leg X-guard considered a primary gateway in the system?
flashcards.answer: Single leg X-guard reliably feeds entries into the ashi-garami family, letting practitioners transition into outside, standard, and inside ashi configurations rather than waiting for opportunistic, low-percentage leg-lock openings.

flashcards.question: What should you do when you lose positional control during a leg attack?
flashcards.answer: Recover a useful entanglement or reset the exchange. Do not chase a finishing grip through uncontrolled movement; the next choice depends on the position and your partner’s reaction.

plausible: Keep the grip and rotate faster
Always force a transition to saddle

flashcards.question: Why must defensive training be developed in parallel with the offensive system?
flashcards.answer: Heel hooks damage knee ligaments without warning pain, so practitioners must understand inside-heel-exposure defense, safe rolling directions, and tap-early protocols to train the system safely and avoid serious injury.

trap: Rotate against the twist to escape

flashcards.question: How does the system's breaking approach differ from explosive leg-lock finishing?
flashcards.answer: It emphasizes gradual, systematic pressure, straightening the leg and retaining the knee line under control, rather than explosive cranking, which preserves position, reduces escape risk, and protects the training partner from injury.

plausible: Sit back the instant you grip
trap: Crank the heel before clearing knee

flashcards.question: What role does the straight ankle lock play within the system?
flashcards.answer: Beyond being a finish, the straight ankle lock serves as a position-maintenance and control tool throughout ashi-garami transitions, helping keep the leg trapped while advancing toward higher-control positions like the saddle.

plausible: Only used as a finishing move
trap: Abandon it once ashi is set
